blocks.x: Even just typing that gave me a headache, so let’s rewind a bit. This isn’t the first time we’ve covered copies of Studio Bitdot’s viral haystack game, Needle In A Haystack Simulator. After several clips of Studio Bitdot’s incremental sorting sim went viral across social media in August, Steam users noticed that several similarly titled games, with inventive titles such as A Needle In a Haystack and Story of The Needle In a Haystack, had suddenly appeared on the platform overnight.

As of writing, I count at least fourteen clones of Studio Bitdot’s original game on Steam. One such game is studio NoGlyph’s Needle In A Haystack, which was released on Steam on September 29. To be clear, NoGlyph’s game doesn’t appear to be in any way vibe-coded, and, for what it’s worth, also doesn’t feature any AI disclaimers on its Steam store page.

Yesterday, on October 17, NoGlyph accused another Needle In A Haystack Simulator clone on Steam of ripping off their code: Little Field Studios’ A Game About Needle In A Haystack, which was released on October 16.

“When we looked through [A Game About Needle In A Haystack’s] files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names,” reads NoGlyph’s post on Steam. “More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn’t exist in their game.”

blocks.c: Game Page Featured Samson A Tyndalston Story Inits

blocks.x: While NoGlyph’s post on Steam doesn’t outright accuse Little Field Studios’ clone of being vibe-coded slop, a comment from the team’s lead dev, Jahvin, on NoGlyph’s Discord confirms exactly how many pieces of its code were copied. Jahvin states that Little Field Studios’ game contains 39 “same-named methods” that are “byte-for-byte identical.”

What Jahvin describes is a classic telltale sign of Claude-assisted decompilation: taking a closed-source game and using AI to make its source code readable, then copy-pasting that code into your own game (or, more likely, asking Claude to do it for you).

While Steam users seem unsympathetic, with some referring to it as “karma” for NoGlyph’s attempt at riding off the coattails of Studio Bitdot’s original Needle In A Haystack Simulator game, the potential vibe-coding element to the story does speak to a larger issue in the indie game scene.

As GameSpark covered in a recent article, a Roblox creator cloned the upcoming indie game Escape the Walls within 24 hours of its dev showing it off to the public. The Roblox creator in question achieved this by simply using a single video of Escape the Walls on X, and then, according to GameSpark, quite brazenly bragged about how said feat was achieved: “Claude did everything for me; I just sat in my chair and watched.”

blocks.c: A Screenshot Of Noglyph's Needle In A Haystack On Steam

blocks.x: Likewise, the devs behind Drunken Goddess Reflux, Alliance Arts, announced that they had cancelled plans to release its upcoming demo on Steam. Why? Because Alliance Arts were concerned that “works imitating or replicating this game’s presentation and gameplay could be quickly produced using AI” if Drunken Goddess Reflux’s demo was released ahead of the full game.

Sadly, it seems like this is the new normal for indie games. Unlike big AAA publishers, indie devs do not have the funding required to legally challenge every single vibe-coded ripoff of their game that appears online, so expect to see fewer demos, fewer early access titles, and, if Escape the Walls’ example is anything to go by, fewer trailers for indie games in the immediate future.
